title: Complex Problem Solving
subject: ICT
description: Practice problem decomposition, pattern recognition, and abstraction (including functions) through the chapter's worksheets, book activities, and Milestone review.

questions.question: What does 'problem decomposition' mean?
questions.explanation: Problem decomposition means breaking a big, difficult problem into smaller, easier parts, so each part is simpler to understand and solve.
options: Breaking a big, difficult problem into smaller, easier parts
Making a small problem bigger and more complicated
Ignoring a problem until it goes away
Solving every problem the exact same way

questions.question: Complete the worksheet blank: 'Problem ___ means breaking a big, difficult problem into smaller and easier parts.'
questions.explanation: The missing word is 'decomposition' — the whole chapter's first big idea is problem decomposition.

questions.question: In the book's bedroom-organizing example, what is the FIRST small task?
questions.explanation: The book lists the bedroom tasks in this order: first put away clothes, then organize books, then clean the desk, and finally vacuum the floor.

questions.question: In the book's bedroom-organizing example, what is the LAST small task?
questions.explanation: The book's order is: put away clothes, organize books, clean the desk, and finally vacuum the floor — vacuuming comes last.

questions.question: Select ALL the smaller tasks the book lists for organizing a bedroom.
questions.explanation: The book breaks 'organize your bedroom' into exactly four smaller tasks: put away clothes, organize books, clean the desk, and vacuum the floor. 'Watch TV' is not one of them.

questions.question: True or False: Problem decomposition makes big tasks more difficult to handle.
questions.explanation: False. This is corrected in the answer key: problem decomposition actually makes big tasks EASIER to manage, not more difficult.

questions.question: True or False: Each small task created by decomposition is usually harder than doing the whole big job at once.
questions.explanation: False — it's the opposite. The book says 'Each small task is much easier than trying to do everything at once.'

questions.question: Why does breaking a big problem into smaller parts make it easier, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Smaller problems are easier to understand and solve than one huge, overwhelming problem — this is the first of the four main reasons the book gives for decomposition.
options: Because smaller problems are easier to understand and solve
Because it takes much longer to finish the task
Because you never have to test any part of the work
Because it hides all the details from you

questions.question: In programming, when creating a game or animation, decomposition means breaking the work into parts such as setting up characters, creating interactions, adding sounds, and adding what else?
questions.explanation: The book explains that programmers break game/animation projects into parts like setting up characters, adding movements, creating interactions, and adding sounds.

questions.question: Fill in the blank from Worksheet L1: '...we break it into parts like setting up characters, adding ___, creating interactions, and adding sounds.'
questions.explanation: The correct word is 'movements' — one of the four parts of building a game or animation mentioned in the chapter.

questions.question: True or False: A real-life application of problem decomposition given in the chapter is cleaning a house room by room instead of all at once.
questions.explanation: True — this is exactly the real-life example the chapter gives for problem decomposition.

questions.question: Which of these best matches the idea of 'testing each part separately' mentioned for game/animation decomposition?
questions.explanation: The book states that breaking a game into parts like characters, movements, interactions, and sounds 'makes the work manageable and helps us test each part separately' — so problems are found in one small piece at a time.
options: Checking each small piece of the project on its own before combining them
Testing the whole finished game only once, at the very end
Never testing anything until a customer complains
Testing only the sounds and ignoring the rest

questions.question: According to the chapter, once you solve one small part of a problem, what can you do with that solution?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that once a part is solved, the solution can be reused in other projects — this is one of the benefits of decomposition.

questions.question: Which statement is a MISCONCEPTION about problem decomposition?
questions.explanation: 'Decomposition makes a problem harder to understand' is false — decomposition does the opposite: it makes big problems easier to understand by splitting them into smaller, manageable parts.
options: Decomposition makes a problem harder to understand
Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller parts
Decomposition lets solved parts be reused later

questions.question: How does decomposition help when 'finding and fixing problems' in a program, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that finding and fixing problems is simpler when a program is divided into parts — for example, debugging by checking small sections rather than the whole program at once.
options: By letting you check small sections instead of the whole program at once
By making every section identical so bugs never occur
By removing the need to test the program

questions.question: Milestone review: What is the main benefit of breaking problems into smaller parts?
questions.explanation: The book's Milestone review confirms the main benefit: it makes smaller problems easier to understand and solve.
options: It makes smaller problems easier to understand and solve
It makes the problem more complicated to understand
It requires more time to complete the entire task
It prevents you from working with other team members

questions.question: Select ALL of the four main reasons the book gives for why decomposition is important.
questions.explanation: The book lists four reasons: smaller problems are easier to solve, teams can work on different parts at the same time, it's easier to find and fix problems, and solved parts can be reused. 'It removes the need for teamwork' is not one of the reasons.
options: Smaller problems are easier to understand and solve
Different people can work on different parts at the same time
It is easier to find and fix a problem in a small section
Once you solve a part, you can reuse that solution in other projects
It removes the need for any teamwork at all

questions.question: How does decomposition help teams finish a project faster, according to the book?
questions.explanation: Because different people can work on different parts of the same project at the same time, the whole project finishes faster — this is one of the four reasons decomposition matters.
options: Different team members can work on different parts at the same time
Only one person is allowed to work on the whole project
The project must be redone from scratch each week
Teams must wait until every other team finishes first

questions.question: True or False: Once you solve a small part of a problem, you can reuse that solution in other projects.
questions.explanation: True — this is one of the chapter's stated benefits of decomposition.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four reasons the book gives for why decomposition is important?
questions.explanation: The book's four reasons are about problems being easier to solve, teamwork, easier debugging, and reusing solutions. 'It makes the project take much longer to finish' is the opposite of what decomposition actually does.
options: Smaller problems are easier to understand and solve
It makes the project take much longer to finish
It is easier to find and fix problems in a small section
Solved parts can be reused in other projects

questions.question: Real-life application: teamwork benefiting from decomposition is compared in the chapter to which example?
questions.explanation: The chapter's example of teamwork benefiting from decomposition is different teams setting up a festival together, each handling a different part.
options: Different teams setting up a festival
One person cleaning an entire house alone
A single chef cooking every dish by themselves
A student doing all homework subjects at once

questions.question: Debugging a program by checking small sections instead of the whole program is described in the chapter as an application of which idea?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives 'debugging a program by checking small sections' as the real-life application of problem decomposition — finding and fixing problems is simpler when they are divided into parts.

questions.question: True or False: According to the chapter, decomposition prevents team members from working on the project at the same time.
questions.explanation: False — decomposition actually ALLOWS different team members to work on different parts simultaneously, which is one of its main benefits.

questions.question: Fun Fact from the chapter: decomposition, as a method of breaking things down, is used in many fields, from programming to which other field mentioned?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Fun Fact says this method (breaking problems into smaller parts) is used in many fields, from programming to project management.

questions.question: 'Think about this' prompt in the chapter asks how often you reuse solutions in daily life. This question connects decomposition to which benefit?
questions.explanation: The chapter's reflection prompt about reusing solutions ties back to the benefit that once a part is solved, its solution can be reused in other projects.
options: Reusing a solved part's solution in other projects

questions.question: Select ALL statements that correctly describe a benefit of problem decomposition mentioned in the chapter.
questions.explanation: All four listed statements are benefits of decomposition explicitly given in the chapter: it lets teams work in parallel, makes problems easier to understand, makes debugging easier, and allows reusing solved parts.
options: It lets team members work on different parts at the same time
It makes problems easier to understand and solve
It makes debugging easier by isolating small sections
It allows a solved part's solution to be reused later
It guarantees a project needs no testing at all

questions.question: The book's example of organizing a school festival breaks the big task into which three main parts?
questions.explanation: The chapter's school festival example is decomposed into three main parts: venue, activities, and food.

questions.question: Which of these tasks belongs to the 'Venue' part of organizing the school festival?
questions.explanation: Venue setup includes booking space, arranging tables, and testing the sound system, according to the chapter.

questions.question: Which of these tasks belongs to the 'Activities and games' part of organizing the school festival?
questions.explanation: 'Activities and games' involve choosing games, preparing materials, and assigning volunteers — assigning volunteers is one of these tasks.

questions.question: Select ALL tasks that belong to the 'Food and drinks' part of the school festival plan.
questions.explanation: 'Food and drinks' requires planning the menu, ordering supplies, and organizing servers. 'Testing the sound system' belongs to the Venue part, not Food.

questions.question: True or False: Testing the sound system is part of the 'Venue' setup in the school festival example.
questions.explanation: True — venue setup specifically includes booking space, arranging tables, and testing the sound system.

questions.question: The chapter gives 'planning a wedding or large event' as a real-life application of decomposing which part of the school festival?
questions.explanation: The chapter connects venue-related planning (booking space, arranging tables, testing sound) to the real-life example of planning a wedding or large event.

questions.question: The chapter's Fun Fact about the 'Activities and games' part says games can make events more:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Fun Fact says 'Games can make events more interactive and fun!' when discussing the activities part of festival planning.

questions.question: What should be considered when planning the 'Food and drinks' part of the festival, according to the chapter's example?
questions.explanation: The chapter's example note for the food part says to 'consider dietary needs and preferences' when planning the menu.
options: The weather forecast for next year

questions.question: True or False: Breaking large projects like the school festival into parts makes them feel more manageable.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter states that breaking tasks into parts makes large projects feel more manageable.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT listed by the chapter as one of the three main parts of organizing the school festival?
questions.explanation: The chapter's three parts are venue, activities, and food — 'ticket sales' is not mentioned as one of the three main parts.

questions.question: In the school festival example, assigning a team to handle each part is given as an example of what?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives 'assigning a team to handle each part' as its example of how the school festival's three parts (venue, activities, food) get organized.
options: Organizing the school festival into venue, activities, and food
Recognizing a repeating pattern in nature
Hiding complex details behind a simple button

questions.question: Select ALL tasks that belong to the 'Activities and games' part of the school festival.
questions.explanation: 'Activities and games' involve choosing games, preparing materials, and assigning volunteers. 'Ordering supplies' belongs to the Food part, not Activities.

questions.question: How many main parts does the school festival example break the big task into?
questions.explanation: The school festival is broken into exactly three main parts: venue, activities, and food.

questions.question: The chapter suggests practising decomposition by creating a digital storybook in which tool?
questions.explanation: The chapter's practice activity says: 'Practice decomposition by creating a digital storybook in Sprite Lab.'

questions.question: Select ALL the parts the chapter suggests breaking a Sprite Lab digital storybook into.
questions.explanation: The chapter's example breaks the storybook down into characters, animations, sounds, and connections.

questions.question: What real-life application does the chapter give for 'writing down tasks to help organize and break them into smaller steps'?
questions.explanation: The chapter's real-life application for writing down and breaking tasks into smaller steps is cooking by following a recipe step by step.
options: Cooking by following a recipe step by step
Watching a movie from start to finish
Painting a picture with no plan

questions.question: True or False: Writing down tasks helps organize and break them into smaller steps.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter states this directly when discussing planning a digital storybook.

questions.question: The chapter suggests choosing a theme for a Sprite Lab story scene, such as Adventure Quest or:
questions.explanation: The chapter gives 'Adventure Quest' and 'Nature Exploration' as example story-scene themes for the Sprite Lab activity.

questions.question: Select ALL steps mentioned for planning a story using decomposition in the chapter.
questions.explanation: The chapter says planning a story using decomposition means you: set the scene, add actions, and add interactions.

questions.question: What real-life application does the chapter compare to planning a story's plot first?
questions.explanation: The chapter compares planning a story using decomposition (setting the scene, then actions, then interactions) to writing a story by planning the plot first.
options: Writing a story by planning the plot first
Building a house without a blueprint

questions.question: Smaller steps, according to the chapter, make complex tasks:
questions.explanation: The chapter states: 'Smaller steps make complex tasks easier to manage,' reinforcing the value of decomposition.

questions.question: Cooking by following a recipe step by step is used in the chapter as a real-life example of what?
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's real-life application example for writing down and breaking tasks into smaller steps — i.e., problem decomposition.

questions.question: True or False: The chapter's Sprite Lab storybook activity breaks work into characters, animations, sounds, and connections, exactly like it breaks a game project into characters, movements, interactions, and sounds.
questions.explanation: True (in spirit) — both activities use the same decomposition approach: splitting a creative digital project into a handful of separate, manageable parts (characters, sounds, and either movements/animations plus interactions/connections).

questions.question: What does 'pattern recognition' mean?
questions.explanation: Pattern recognition means finding things that repeat or are similar to each other.
options: Finding things that repeat or are similar
Breaking a big problem into smaller parts
Hiding complex details from the user
Writing a named group of instructions

questions.question: Worksheet blank: 'When you spot a ___, you can use the same solution multiple times instead of starting from scratch every time.'
questions.explanation: The missing word is 'pattern' — recognizing a pattern lets you reuse a solution instead of solving the same type of problem from scratch each time.

questions.question: Milestone review: Which of these is an example of pattern recognition in daily life?
questions.explanation: The Milestone review confirms that days of the week repeating every seven days regularly is the correct example of pattern recognition in daily life.
options: Days of the week repeating every seven days regularly
Trying a completely new method for each task you do
Making every paper flower using a different technique
Creating a unique schedule for every single Monday

questions.question: Worksheet L2 tick question: Which of these shows a pattern?
questions.explanation: 'Skip counting: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10' shows a clear, repeating pattern (adding 2 each time). Random numbers and things with no order are not patterns.

questions.question: Select ALL examples of patterns in daily life mentioned in the chapter.
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions several daily-life patterns: days of the week repeating every seven days, songs repeating verses and choruses, and building blocks/floor tiles creating repeating patterns.
options: Days of the week repeating every seven days
Floor tiles creating a repeating pattern
A brand new random password every second

questions.question: In math, the chapter says skip counting like 2, 4, 6, 8 is an example of what?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that in math, skip counting follows patterns like 2, 4, 6, 8 — an example of pattern recognition.

questions.question: True or False: Recognizing patterns can help with time management, according to the chapter's Fun Fact.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter's Fun Fact says recognizing patterns can help with time management.

questions.question: The book states there are three main types of patterns. Which of these is the FIRST type?
questions.explanation: The book's first pattern type is 'repeating actions,' where the same steps happen multiple times, like moving a sprite forward ten times using a loop.
options: Repeating actions, like moving a sprite forward ten times
Similar problems that use the same approach, like checking if a number is even
Random, unpredictable events with no order

questions.question: The book's SECOND type of pattern is 'similar problems that use the same approach.' Which example does it give?
questions.explanation: The book's example for this pattern type is checking if any number is even, using the same method: divide by 2 and check for remainders.
options: Checking if a number is even by dividing by 2 and checking the remainder
Moving a sprite forward ten times with a loop
Turning right 90 degrees four times to draw a square
Hiding a TV's circuits behind a remote control

questions.question: The book's THIRD type of pattern is 'sequences with predictable patterns.' Which example does it give?
questions.explanation: The book's example is the sequence 2, 4, 6, 8, where you add 2 each time to find the next number.
options: Moving a sprite forward ten times with a loop
Checking if a number is even
Drawing a hexagon by turning 60 degrees

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the chapter's three main types of patterns?
questions.explanation: The chapter's three pattern types are: repeating actions, similar problems using the same approach, and sequences with predictable patterns. 'Totally random, unpredictable events' is the opposite of a pattern.
options: Similar problems using the same approach

questions.question: Using patterns, you can solve similar problems how, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states: 'Using patterns, you can solve similar problems efficiently.'

questions.question: True or False: In programming, patterns help reuse solutions without rewriting code.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter states that in programming, patterns help reuse solutions without rewriting code, giving loops as the example.

questions.question: The chapter says recognizing patterns lets you work how?
questions.explanation: The chapter repeats this idea at several points: recognizing patterns helps you work smarter, not harder.

questions.question: Select ALL items that are TRUE about pattern recognition, based on the chapter.
questions.explanation: All four statements are directly supported by the chapter: patterns mean finding repeats/similarities, they let you reuse solutions efficiently, they help you work smarter, and they can aid time management. Pattern recognition does not mean hiding details — that is abstraction.
options: Pattern recognition means finding things that repeat or are similar
Recognizing patterns lets you reuse a solution efficiently
Recognizing patterns helps you work smarter, not harder
Recognizing patterns can help with time management
Pattern recognition means hiding complex details from the user

questions.question: Crossword clue: 'Days of the week follow a weekly ___.' What is the answer?
questions.explanation: The crossword's answer is 'pattern' — days of the week repeating every seven days is a classic example of a pattern.

questions.question: The chapter mentions building blocks and floor tiles as examples of what?
questions.explanation: The chapter states 'Building blocks and floor tiles create repeating patterns,' giving them as real-world visual examples of pattern recognition.

questions.question: Worksheet L2 tick question: In programming, what do we use to repeat the same action many times?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'a loop.' Loops let you repeat an action many times without writing the same code over and over.
options: Write the same code over and over

questions.question: Crossword clue: 'To do something again and again, you use a ___.'
questions.explanation: The crossword answer is 'loop' — loops let a program repeat an action again and again.

questions.question: True or False: Instead of writing 'move forward' ten separate times, you can use a loop that repeats the move command ten times.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter's example shows exactly this: instead of writing 'move forward' ten times, you use a loop that repeats it.

questions.question: The chapter gives 'algorithms for sorting data' as a real-life application of which pattern idea?
questions.explanation: The chapter connects 'algorithms for sorting data' to the pattern idea of similar problems using the same approach (like checking if numbers are even).
options: Similar problems using the same approach

questions.question: True or False: Sequences with predictable patterns help solve problems quickly.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter states this directly: 'Sequences with predictable patterns help solve problems quickly.'

questions.question: According to the chapter, checking if a number is even uses which programming approach?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that checking if any number is even 'uses the same method: divide by 2 and check for remainders' — an example of recognizing similar problems that use the same approach.
options: Dividing by 2 and checking the remainder

questions.question: Which of these is the BEST reason programmers use loops instead of repeating the same line of code many times?
questions.explanation: Loops let you recognize a repeating pattern and reuse the same instruction efficiently, instead of writing (and maintaining) the same line of code over and over.
options: Loops let you reuse the same instruction efficiently instead of repeating code
Loops make the program run on a different computer
Loops are required by law in every program

questions.question: The chapter's example code repeats a 'move' command 10 pixels to which direction?
questions.explanation: The Sprite Lab example code block shown in the chapter repeats 'move 10 pixels East' inside a loop.

questions.question: True or False: 'Think about this' in the chapter asks how patterns in nature inspire technology.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter includes exactly this reflection prompt when discussing sequences with predictable patterns.

questions.question: Instead of writing the same code multiple times, recognizing a pattern in programming lets you:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that in programming, patterns help reuse solutions without rewriting code — for example, using loops to repeat actions in coding.
options: Delete the program and start over
Slow down the computer on purpose
Remove all sprites from the project

questions.question: Activity 2's first shape is drawn by repeating 'draw a line forward, then turn right 90 degrees' four times. What shape is this?
questions.explanation: Turning 90 degrees four times and drawing a line each time creates a square, which is exactly what the activity's answer should be.

questions.question: Activity 2's second shape is drawn by repeating 'draw a line forward, then turn right 120 degrees' three times. What shape is this?
questions.explanation: Turning 120 degrees three times and drawing a line each time creates a triangle.

questions.question: Activity 3 draws a shape by repeating 'draw a line forward, then turn right 60 degrees' six times. What shape is this?
questions.explanation: Turning 60 degrees six times and drawing a line each time creates a hexagon, matching the diagram shown in the chapter.

questions.question: According to the chapter, how do you calculate the turning angle needed to draw any regular polygon?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the general rule: the turning angle equals 360 divided by the number of sides of the shape.
options: 360 divided by the number of sides
180 divided by the number of sides
The number of sides multiplied by 10

questions.question: What is 360 divided by 4 — the turning angle used to draw the square in Activity 2?
questions.explanation: 360 ÷ 4 = 90, which matches the 90-degree turns used to draw the square.

questions.question: What is 360 divided by 3 — the turning angle used to draw the triangle in Activity 2?
questions.explanation: 360 ÷ 3 = 120, which matches the 120-degree turns used to draw the triangle.

questions.question: What is 360 divided by 6 — the turning angle used to draw the hexagon in Activity 3?
questions.explanation: 360 ÷ 6 = 60, which matches the 60-degree turns used to draw the hexagon.

questions.question: True or False: The rule 'turn 360 divided by the number of sides' applies to all regular polygons, according to the chapter's Fun Fact.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter's Fun Fact states that this rule applies to all regular polygons.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say 'Now you have one solution that works for any shape' after showing the repeat-and-turn rule?
questions.explanation: Because recognizing the repeating pattern (draw a line, then turn 360/sides degrees) lets the SAME instructions work for a square, triangle, hexagon, or any other regular polygon — this is the power of pattern recognition.
options: Because the same repeating pattern of instructions works for any regular polygon
Because the shape only needs to be drawn once ever
Because computers cannot draw more than one shape
Because all shapes are secretly circles

questions.question: Using the chapter's general formula, what turning angle would be needed to draw a regular pentagon (5 sides)?
questions.explanation: This applies the chapter's own stated rule (360 ÷ number of sides) to a new shape it doesn't explicitly draw: 360 ÷ 5 = 72 degrees.

questions.question: What are the TWO repeating steps that all shape-drawing instructions in the chapter share?
questions.explanation: The chapter states: 'All shapes repeat the same two steps: draw a line and turn.' Only the number of repeats and the turning angle change.

questions.question: In Activity 2 and 3, what tool were students asked to use to trace the shapes?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Activity 2 instructions ask students to 'trace with a ruler and pencil' to draw the shapes.

questions.question: Select ALL shapes explicitly drawn using the repeat-and-turn pattern in the chapter's activities.
questions.explanation: The chapter's activities explicitly draw a square (90°), a triangle (120°), and a hexagon (60°) using the repeat-and-turn pattern. A pentagon is not explicitly drawn in the chapter.

questions.question: True or False: To draw a shape with more sides, you need a completely different, unrelated set of instructions each time.
questions.explanation: False — the whole point of pattern recognition here is that ONE general instruction pattern (repeat: draw line, turn 360/sides degrees) works for any regular polygon, no matter how many sides it has.

questions.question: What does 'abstraction' mean in this chapter?
questions.explanation: Abstraction means hiding complex details and showing only what's important.
options: Hiding complex details and showing only what's important
Breaking a big problem into smaller parts
Finding things that repeat or are similar
Writing the same code many times

questions.question: Worksheet blank: 'Abstraction means hiding ___ details and showing only what's important.'
questions.explanation: The missing word is 'complex' — abstraction hides complex details.

questions.question: Milestone review: What does a TV remote demonstrate about abstraction?
questions.explanation: The Milestone review's correct answer is: 'You can control a complex machine with simple buttons.' You don't need to understand the circuits inside.
options: You can control a complex machine with simple buttons
You must understand all circuits to change the channel
You need to know the technology inside to use it
You have to write code to make the remote function

questions.question: Worksheet L2 tick question: Which is the BEST example of abstraction?
questions.explanation: Using a smartphone without knowing the millions of lines of code running underneath is the chapter's best example of abstraction.
options: Using a smartphone without knowing millions of code lines
Knowing all the circuits inside a TV

questions.question: True or False: A TV remote is an example of abstraction because you can control a complex machine with simple buttons.
questions.explanation: True — this is confirmed in the worksheet answer key.

questions.question: True or False: Abstraction requires you to understand all the complex details inside a device to use it.
questions.explanation: False. The answer key corrects this: abstraction means you DON'T need to understand all the complex details to use a device.

questions.question: True or False (Milestone review): When using abstraction, you need to understand all the complex details inside a device like a TV to use it.
questions.explanation: False — this is exactly the misconception the Milestone review corrects; abstraction lets you use a device WITHOUT understanding all its complex details.

questions.question: When you press a button on a TV remote to change the channel, what don't you need to know about, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter says you don't need to know about the circuits, signals, and technology inside the TV — the remote gives you a simple way to control a complex machine.
options: The circuits, signals, and technology inside the TV

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is hidden underneath a smartphone's simple icons and buttons?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that hidden underneath a smartphone's simple icons and buttons are millions of lines of code.

questions.question: Select ALL benefits abstraction gives programmers, according to the chapter.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists several benefits of abstraction in programming: focusing on what something does instead of how, reusing code without rewriting it, making complex programs easier to understand, and letting people work on different parts independently.
options: Focus on what something does instead of how it does it
Make complex programs easier to understand
Work on different parts of a program independently
Force everyone to write the exact same code

questions.question: The chapter's real-life application of abstraction mentions mobile apps with simple interfaces but complex:
questions.explanation: The chapter's real-life application example is 'mobile apps with simple interfaces but complex backends.'

questions.question: Which of these statements about abstraction is FALSE?
questions.explanation: 'You must understand every circuit inside a device before using it' is false — that is the opposite of abstraction, which hides those complex details so you don't need to understand them.
options: Abstraction hides complex details and shows only what's important
You must understand every circuit inside a device before using it
A TV remote lets you control a complex machine simply
In programming, abstraction helps simplify and reuse code

questions.question: In programming, abstraction lets people work on different parts of a program independently. Why is this useful, based on the chapter?
questions.explanation: Because abstraction hides the complex internal details of each part, different programmers don't need to worry about all the details of parts they aren't working on — they can focus on their own piece.
options: Because they don't need to worry about every detail of parts they aren't working on
Because it stops all programmers from ever meeting
Because it deletes unfinished code automatically
Because it prevents any code reuse

questions.question: True or False: In programming, abstraction helps simplify and reuse code.
questions.explanation: True — the chapter states this directly as one of abstraction's key benefits.

questions.question: Milestone fill-in-the-blank: 'Abstraction means hiding complex details and showing only what's ___.'
questions.explanation: The missing word is 'important' — abstraction shows only what's important while hiding the rest.

questions.question: Which everyday object does the chapter use TWICE as an example of abstraction — once as the main example and once in the recap?
questions.explanation: The TV remote is used as the chapter's main abstraction example and is repeated in the chapter's recap of the three big concepts.

questions.question: What is a 'function' in programming, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: A function is a named group of instructions that performs a specific task in programming.
options: A named group of instructions that performs a specific task
A random number generated by the computer
A picture used as a background
A password used to log in

questions.question: Worksheet blank: 'A ___ is a named group of instructions that performs a specific task in programming.'
questions.explanation: The missing word is 'function.'

questions.question: How many steps does the chapter's sandwich recipe have (get bread, spread chutney, add vegetables, close bread, cut in half)?
questions.explanation: The sandwich recipe has exactly 5 steps: get bread, spread chutney, add vegetables, close bread, and cut in half.

questions.question: Without using a function, how many total steps would you write out to make 3 sandwiches, each needing the same 5 steps?
questions.explanation: Without a function, you must write all 5 steps for each of the 3 sandwiches: 5 x 3 = 15 steps total, as the chapter explains.

questions.question: With a function called 'makeSandwich,' how many times do you need to write out the 5 sandwich-making steps?
questions.explanation: With a function, you write the 5 steps only ONCE inside 'makeSandwich,' then call 'makeSandwich' as many times as needed.

questions.question: Milestone MCQ: How many times do you need to write the sandwich-making steps when using a function?

It means removing all buttons from a remote
It has nothing to do with hiding details

questions.question: The chapter says abstraction lets programmers 'focus on what something does instead of how it does it.' Which everyday example best matches this idea?
questions.explanation: Using a smartphone icon to open an app is a good match: you know WHAT it does (opens the app) without knowing HOW the underlying code works.
options: Tapping a smartphone icon without knowing the underlying code
Reading every line of a program's source code before using it
Building a TV from individual electronic components
Memorizing a device's entire circuit diagram

questions.question: A student claims: 'Using a function always makes a program run on a different computer.' Why is this false, based on the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter never says functions change WHERE a program runs — functions are about organizing and reusing code (fewer repeated steps, easier updates), not about which computer runs it.
options: Functions are about reusing and organizing code, not about which computer runs it
Functions can only run on smartphones

questions.question: Comparing 15 total steps (without a function) to writing 5 steps once (with 'makeSandwich'), what is saved by using the function?
questions.explanation: Using the function saves the effort of writing (and later updating) the same 5 steps three separate times — you write them once and reuse them by simply calling the function's name.
options: The effort of writing and updating the same steps multiple times
The number of vegetables in the sandwich

questions.question: Select ALL statements that correctly compare 'with function' vs 'without function' for making 3 sandwiches, based on the chapter.
questions.explanation: Without a function, you repeat all 5 steps for each of the 3 sandwiches (15 steps total). With a function, you write the 5 steps once and call 'makeSandwich' three times — and if you want to change the recipe, you only update it once.
options: Without a function, you write 15 steps in total
With a function, you write the 5 steps only once
With a function, you only update the recipe in one place if it changes
Without a function, you write only 5 steps in total

questions.question: A student thinks giving a function a name like 'setupGame' is just for decoration and doesn't matter. Why is this wrong, based on the chapter?
questions.explanation: The function's name is how you call and reuse the whole group of instructions later — without a clear name, you couldn't easily reuse or identify what the group of instructions does.
options: The name lets you call and reuse the instructions later by referring to it
The name changes the colours in the game
The name has no effect on anything at all
The name determines how many sprites the game has

questions.question: Why does the chapter connect 'functions help you reuse code blocks' with efficiency in programming?
questions.explanation: Reusing existing code blocks (via functions) means programmers don't have to recreate the same instructions every time they're needed, saving time and reducing repeated work.
options: Because it saves time by avoiding recreating the same instructions repeatedly
Because it makes the code run in a different language
Because it removes all sprites from a game
Because it deletes the function immediately after use

questions.question: A classmate mixes up examples and says 'using a loop in coding' illustrates abstraction rather than pattern recognition. What is the mistake?
questions.explanation: The chapter's recap specifically gives 'using a loop in coding to repeat actions efficiently' as the example for PATTERN RECOGNITION (reusing solutions), not abstraction (hiding complex details).
options: Using a loop illustrates pattern recognition (reusing solutions), not abstraction
There is no mistake, both are correct
Loops are not related to any of the three concepts

questions.question: Select ALL examples that the chapter's recap correctly pairs with problem decomposition.
questions.explanation: The recap pairs problem decomposition with: 'vacuuming is one task in cleaning a house' and 'decorating a party by dividing tasks among friends.' The TV remote example belongs to abstraction, not decomposition.
options: Vacuuming is one task in cleaning a house
Decorating a party by dividing tasks among friends
Using a TV remote without understanding all circuits

questions.topic: Milestone Review: Fill in the Blanks
questions.question: In the Milestone word bank (important, smaller, function, easier, vacuum, repeat), which word correctly completes BOTH the decomposition blank AND connects to 'making tasks manageable'?
questions.explanation: 'Easier' fits the decomposition sentence ('...smaller, easier parts') and reflects the overall idea that decomposition makes big tasks more manageable, matching the corrected True/False statement about decomposition.

questions.topic: Milestone Review: Fill in the Blanks
questions.question: True or False: The Milestone review's fill-in-the-blank word bank and its True/False section both test the same three big concepts of the chapter.
questions.explanation: True — both sections revisit problem decomposition, pattern recognition, and abstraction (including functions), just using different question formats.

questions.topic: Milestone Review: Tick the Correct Option
questions.question: In Milestone MCQ #4, why is 'You need to write the steps fifteen times in total' the WRONG answer, even though '15' does appear in the chapter's sandwich example?
questions.explanation: 15 is the total step count WITHOUT using a function (5 steps x 3 sandwiches). The question asks how many times you write the steps WITH a function, which is only once — 15 is a distractor based on the earlier no-function scenario.
options: 15 is the without-function total; with a function you only write the steps once
15 is actually the correct answer to this question
The number 15 never appears anywhere in the chapter

questions.topic: Milestone Review: Tick the Correct Option
questions.question: What common thread links all 5 questions in the Milestone 'Tick the correct option' section?
questions.explanation: All 5 questions test understanding of the chapter's three big ideas (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction) and the role of functions, checking that students grasp WHY each concept is useful.
options: They all test understanding of decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and functions
They are all about crossword puzzles
They are all unrelated trivia questions

questions.question: Worksheet L1's True/False item (c) states a character jumping 20 times without functions needs 80 lines of code. Which idea does this best connect to from elsewhere in the chapter?
questions.explanation: This connects to the same abstraction/functions idea as the 'makeSandwich' example: without a function, repeated actions (jumping, or making sandwiches) require the same instructions to be written out multiple times, leading to many more lines of code.
options: The makeSandwich idea: without functions, repeated actions need repeated code
The idea that abstraction never applies to games
The idea that patterns never repeat in code
The idea that decomposition removes the need for functions

questions.question: Worksheet L1 asks students to identify five vocabulary words. Which pairing of blank-and-answer is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Blank (e), 'A ___ is a named group of instructions that performs a specific task in programming,' is correctly filled with 'function.'

questions.question: A student fills in the crossword clue 'Instructions that tell the computer what to do' with 'LOOP' instead of 'CODES.' What is the mistake?
questions.explanation: 'Loop' refers to repeating an action, while 'codes' (the correct answer) refers to the instructions themselves that tell a computer what to do — these are related but different ideas in the crossword.
options: 'Codes' means instructions; 'loop' means repeating an action — they are different
There is no mistake, both words are identical in meaning
Crosswords do not have unique correct answers

questions.question: Why does Worksheet L2 include a crossword puzzle in addition to the tick-the-correct-option questions?
questions.explanation: The crossword reinforces the chapter's key vocabulary (simple, tasks, codes, pattern, loop) in a different, more playful format than multiple-choice questions, helping students recall the words themselves.
options: To reinforce the chapter's key vocabulary in a different, playful format
Because multiple-choice questions are not allowed in ICT
Because crosswords replace the need for an answer key
Because vocabulary is unrelated to the chapter

questions.topic: Step Ahead: Plan Your Dream Birthday Party
questions.question: A student wraps 5 gift bags and writes 4 steps for EACH bag separately (20 lines total), then says 'I used a function.' What is wrong with this claim?
questions.explanation: Writing all 20 lines separately for each bag means the steps were repeated 5 times without reuse — that is the WITHOUT-function approach. Using a function would mean writing the 4 steps only once and calling it 5 times.
options: Writing 20 separate lines means the without-function approach was used, not a function
This is correct — that is exactly how functions work
Functions require exactly 20 lines every time
Gift bags cannot use functions at all

questions.topic: Step Ahead: Plan Your Dream Birthday Party
questions.question: How does 'Plan Your Dream Birthday Party' connect Part 2 (pattern recognition) to Part 3 (abstraction with functions)?
questions.explanation: In Part 2, recognizing that all 5 invitation cards need the same repeated information is a pattern; in Part 3, that same idea of repetition (5 gift bags needing the same 4 steps) is handled even more efficiently using a function, showing how pattern recognition and abstraction work together.
options: Both parts deal with repeated, similar tasks — Part 3 handles the repetition with a function
The two parts are completely unrelated
Part 2 is about food, and Part 3 is about decorations
Part 3 removes the need for any invitations

questions.topic: Step Ahead: Plan Your Dream Birthday Party
questions.question: Select ALL parts of the 'Plan Your Dream Birthday Party' activity that are correctly matched to their concept.
questions.explanation: The three parts are correctly matched as: Part 1 = Problem Decomposition (break into 3 tasks), Part 2 = Pattern Recognition (5 identical invitation cards), Part 3 = Abstraction (wrapGift function). Matching Part 1 to abstraction is incorrect.
